items.item: Framing all five join types (regular, interval, temporal, lookup, delta) as answers to a single axis — how much state does the join need — is what makes the whole taxonomy coherent rather than a disconnected list of syntax variants to memorize separately.

at.step: Reveal: a regular join keeps every row forever

items.item: Upsert mode's dependence on a unique key is not a minor implementation detail — it's the precise reason retract mode exists at all as a genuine alternative, not a strictly worse one: retract works without any key, at the cost of extra messages per update.

at.step: Reveal: upsert and retract agree on the table, not the cost

items.item: Interval and temporal joins both avoid a regular join's unbounded state, but by genuinely different mechanisms — a real time window versus a per-row point-in-time version lookup — which is why this topic presents them as two separate reveals rather than variations of the same idea.

at.step: Reveal: interval and temporal joins each bound state differently

items.item: Delta joins are deliberately framed as newer and less settled than the other four join types, since Flink's own documentation covers them only through a configuration-option reference and a release announcement, not a dedicated conceptual docs page the way regular and interval joins have.

at.step: Reveal: lookup and delta joins trade state for a different cost

items.item: Materialised tables' freshness-driven refresh-mode choice mirrors the same state-versus-cost tradeoff running through the whole topic: a continuous job (more resource cost, less latency) versus a periodic batch job (less cost, more latency), the identical shape as the join taxonomy's own tradeoff.

at.step: Reveal: materialised tables and process table functions

items.item: This topic's hook (a stream is secretly a table) and the recap's close (same table, different encodings) are the same observation made twice — first as an open reframing, then as the settled idea the whole reel built toward through the changelog-mode and join-taxonomy reveals.

at.step: Hook: a stream is secretly a table the whole time

items.item: The toy changelog-mode interpreter and join-state models are deliberately simplified standalone demonstrations, not ports of Flink's actual SQL planner or join-operator internals, and every figure shown is this run's own measured output, not a cited Flink benchmark.

items.item: This topic uses the state-backend and checkpoint mechanics from topics 20-23 directly as a given foundation — the dynamic-table model doesn't reopen how Flink actually stores a join's kept state, only how much of it each join type needs to keep.
